# Review

Opposite-argument test: could someone informed reasonably argue that a fixed rule can use incident lessons *without* anyone identifying when they apply? Hardly. Applying a lesson already involves recognizing that it applies, so the "only if" condition is nearly analytic.

The note does make contestable claims, but the title does not. One is that a standing "check past incidents" instruction can stay fixed while its effective content grows; someone could argue that each incident should add a specific checklist item. The other is that a lesson transfers through a structural feature, such as two sources sharing an origin when the claim depends on their independence, and not through name-based lookup. The title presupposes the first claim in its subject and leaves the second out. This matches the gate's presupposed-claim pattern: the hard point sits in the subject and the predicate is weak.

# Review

The body is short and consistent. A standing rule such as "check past incidents" tells the reviewer where to look but not which earlier failure applies. The citation example shows that a lesson transfers through a structural feature (shared origin behind supposedly independent support), which a lookup by source name would miss. The test of success is whether the reviewer separates apparent corroboration from independent support. The incident changes what the review must distinguish, not the rule.

The H1 broadly matches this topic, but it gives the identifying role to the wrong agent. "It can identify" refers back to the rule, while the body explicitly denies that the rule identifies anything and gives that work to the reviewer. A version such as "A fixed review rule can absorb new incident lessons when the reviewer recognizes the failure's structural feature" would match the body.

# Review

The note belongs in `kb/theory/`. It makes a transferable, truth-apt claim about review rules and incident learning. It names no Commonplace system choice that would need scoping, and it is not a procedure or a design record. Its read is universal by default, which the contract allows. It cites no sources, so the source-grounding bound does not apply. It does not link into `kb/work/`, and nothing it says is defensive padding.

The main gap is in how the claim is stated. The title says the *rule* must be able to identify when a lesson applies. The description and the body say the rule leaves that identification to the *reviewer*, and they show the reviewer doing it. The collection's explanatory-reach guidance treats the claim surfaces as obligations and asks for a claim whose failure can be stated exactly. Here, which party carries the condition changes what would refute the claim, so the mismatch is a WARN.

Secondary points are advisory. The note shows only the side of its "only if" where the condition holds. It has no boundary or open-question section for the case where the condition fails. It also has no links to neighbouring theory.

The wiki-citation example makes the mechanism concrete, and the final paragraph states the test the claim implies.

The unmet instruction concerns traversal. The template ends with a Relevant Notes footer, and the Writing Shape section asks for links to adjacent notes where the relationship helps traversal. With no links, the note is isolated from the material it refines.

Scope is a lesser concern. The note leaves its dependence on the reviewer's ability to abstract features implicit. The instruction allows the Scope section to be omitted, and the body gestures at the failure case, so this does not raise the outcome.

# Review

## Summary

The note has a partial mechanism. The instruction names a location, not relevance, and a lesson transfers through a structural feature that a lookup by name would miss. The second point is constrained and testable. However, the title's "only if" is nearly true by definition, so it adds little content. The body's main move, that a reviewer following the unchanged rule "could still recognize" the lesson, does not say what makes recognition possible or what would make it fail. Without that, nothing in the argument says when an incident would show that the rule must change. The closing sentence's contrast is therefore not hard to vary.

The likely intended reading is "the review applying it", but the text does not say so, and the agent of identification drifts from the rule to the reviewer between the title and the body.

# Friction check: fixed review rules and when incident lessons apply

**Central claim (one sentence):** A fixed instruction to consult past incidents can stay unchanged as incidents accumulate, but a new incident helps only when the reviewer recognizes which distinction it teaches applies to the case at hand, so incidents change what the review must distinguish rather than the rule.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The note asks for three things at once: the rule stays fixed, new lessons get used, and applicability is judged case by case. These can coexist if the applicability judgment comes from something other than the rule text. The note implies that but does not name it. The claim concretizes to one thing. There is a strain, not a contradiction: the title makes the rule responsible for identifying applicability, while the body says the rule cannot do that and gives the job to the reviewer.

## Thinnest joints

The two UNSUPPORTED joints rank first because they carry the note's conclusion. One is the claim that the rule need not change. The other is the claim that a reviewer following the unchanged rule could still recognize the connection. Neither names the mechanism that turns an unchanged rule plus an incident record into a recognized applicability. The note's first paragraph rules out the instruction as that mechanism. The THIN joints come next. The "only if" in the title is motivated by a gap but not shown to be necessary, and it shifts subject from rule to reviewer. The retrieval/distinction contrast is directionally right but phrased as exclusive. The example's internal logic is the strongest part and holds.

## For the human
Start with the closing sentence: name what lets a reviewer under the unchanged rule recognize applicability. If that capability depends on how incidents are recorded, it may undercut "the review rule need not change".

# Critique: fixed review rules and when incident lessons apply

**Note:** kb/theory/fixed-review-rules-must-identify-when-incident-lessons-apply.md
**Central commitment:** A fixed instruction such as "check past incidents before publication" can keep absorbing lessons from new incidents without being rewritten, provided the review can identify the feature that makes an earlier failure bear on the page at hand.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

The opposing stance is the codification position, as in post-incident checklist practice in aviation and medicine and as in this KB's own move of turning observed failures into explicit checks. Its argument has three steps.

First, the note's condition has the wrong bearer. The title says the *rule* must "identify when they apply", but "Check past incidents before publication" identifies nothing. The note concedes this: the instruction "does not tell the reviewer which earlier failure bears on the page at hand." All of the identifying work is done by the reviewer. So if the rule stays fixed, the title's condition is unmet. If the condition is met, it is met by something other than the rule.

Second, the example hides a change. The double-citation lesson transfers only after someone has stated it as "the sources share an origin and the claim relies on their independence." That feature-level formulation is not in the raw incident ("these two citations copied one report"). Someone has to produce and store it. Wherever it lives (an incident log entry, reviewer training, an appended check), something other than the bare rule changed. The rule stays fixed only because the change has moved elsewhere.

Third, recognition by an unaided reviewer does not scale. As incidents accumulate, a reviewer told only "check past incidents" must hold every abstracted lesson and match it against every page. That is the recall-and-match load checklists exist to remove. The codification position says the reliable remedy is to write the applicability test into the rule: "when a claim depends on independent sources, verify they do not share an origin." On that view the note's final sentence, "not that the review rule must change", is wrong as a general claim. It holds only where the incident load is small and the reviewer is strong.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.** The note grants the first step's premise: the instruction "tells the reviewer where to look" but not which failure applies. It also anticipates surface lookup failing ("A lookup by source name would miss that connection"). Its proposed test, whether the reviewer "distinguishes apparent corroboration from independent support", correctly puts the success criterion on recognition rather than retrieval.

The note does not engage the remaining steps. It does not say where the abstracted applicability condition lives or who produces it. It does not consider the alternative of writing that condition into the rule. It also gives no condition for when unaided recognition is adequate. Its conclusion that the rule need not change is asserted, not argued against codification. The title compounds this by assigning the identifying capacity to the rule, which the body then shows the rule lacks.

The attack does not fully land. The note's narrower point survives: retrieving an incident is not the same as applying its lesson, and an incident's value lies in the distinction it teaches, not its surface particulars. A fixed pointer rule plus a capable reviewer can work in the single example given.

## Constructive findings

- Make the title and body name the same bearer. Either the claim is about the reviewer ("a reviewer under a fixed rule can use new incidents only if it recognizes the feature that makes them apply"), or it is about the rule, in which case the rule must carry the applicability condition.
- State where the feature-level formulation of an incident is stored and how a raw incident becomes one. That is the step that makes recognition possible, and it is currently implicit in the example.
- Engage codification directly: give the condition under which leaving the rule fixed is adequate (few incidents, a reviewer able to abstract) and the condition under which the applicability test should be written into the rule (many incidents, weaker or varied reviewers, a high cost of a miss).
- Align the description with the body's conclusion. The description presents the fixed rule as a burden on the reviewer; the body presents it as sufficient.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- The note's claim risks tautology: "a lesson can be used only if one can tell when it applies" is true of any lesson under any rule. Its non-trivial content is the further claim that the rule need not change. That claim is the one the note argues least.
- One example supports a general "can remain the review rule" claim. A second case would show whether the result depends on the incident being as cleanly abstractable as citation independence, for instance one where the applicable feature is contested.

**Central commitment (one sentence):** A fixed review instruction to consult past incidents can carry lessons from new incidents only when the reviewer recognizes the structural feature that makes an earlier failure bear on the case at hand. Retrieval alone does not carry them, and the rule need not change.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment combines a necessity claim ("only if" the reviewer identifies applicability) with a stability claim (the rule can stay fixed). The necessity side rests on three premises: the instruction does not supply applicability; surface lookup misses structural matches; and no cheaper route than identification exists. The stability side rests on two premises: reviewer recognition can carry the transfer, and incident accumulation does not force a rule change. A further premise is that the proposed success test detects transfer. The note attributes identification to the rule in its title and to the reviewer in its body; that ambiguity is surfaced as a separate premise because the commitment changes depending on which reading holds.

No premise fails globally. The two premises at the note's ends hold: the generic instruction gives no applicability, and lookup by name misses the example. The doubtful premises all accept boundary conditions. One condition is the incident-record scale at which a fixed rule remains workable. Another is that incident records state mechanisms. Another is a budget that rules out applying every lesson everywhere. The fourth is a test that separates the lesson's contribution from general reviewer skill. The short note states none of these conditions, so its stability claim reads as universal.

## For the human

Look first at the claim that the rule need not change: as incidents accumulate, the case for indexing them by triggering feature grows. The note's file name ("rules must identify") already points the opposite way from its closing sentence.
